newsitem.title: USA: Mass. takes up deregulation, bonds and development.
newsitem.headline: Mass. takes up deregulation, bonds and development.

text.p: Deregulation of the electric industry gets rotunda attention this week at the Massachusetts State House.
On Wednesday, the state's Government Regulation Committee and the Energy Committee meet jointly to hear the major proposals deregulating the electric utility industry.

Gov. William Weld, whose administration has been working to open the market to competition for the past year, is expected to testify on behalf of his plan, which calls for but does not mandate a 10 percent drop in consumer electric bills.
Last week, the special commission on electric utility restructuring issued its plan assuring that all Massachusetts residents receive a 10 percent break on bills starting Jan 1, 1998.

Lowering rates has been a sticking point in the intense debate between utility companies and lawmakers because of the almost $5 billion debt utility companies piled up over the past 30 years. Those debts stem largely from the construction of nuclear power plants during the1970s that failed to turn profits.
Sen. John O'Brien, D-Andover, the commission co-chairman, will defend the commission's plan and its call to keep a closer eye on utilities' attempts to recover those costs.
The Committee on Housing and Urban Development is also set to take testimony Thursday on a $375 million housing bond bill, a week later than previously reported.
The bill would provide $220 million for modernization of existing housing, $75 million to acquire and rehabilitate old buildings, and fund to help non-profit groups to buy and preserve properities.

Meanwhile, this week also marks the debut of the House Committee on Long Term Debt and Capital Expenditures. House Speaker Thomas Finneran convinced his chamber to set up the committee as a way of making the Legislature an equal partner with the governor in deciding how state dollars should be spent once long-term debt is authorized for capital projects.

Previously lawmakers authorized long-term debt for projects important to their districts with the luxury of knowing that the governor, not them, made the final decision about those dollars would actually be authorized. The Senate has not created a similar panel.

The Committee took testimony Monday on the development of the U.S. Army's abandoned installation, Fort Devens in Ayer, Mass. The state now owns the land and an intermodal transportation facility is in the works. Gov. Weld has filed a bill capping the amount of money the state's land bank can spend on development projects on that site at $200 million.

Also Monday, the Insurance Committee is to hear a measure requiring insurance companies to invest in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. The proposal by Sen. Dianne Wilkerson, requires banks to reinvest in communities in which they do business.
